title: Chardi kala in the century
hookLine: a people hunted for decades sang at night

lines: TWO WORDS NEAR THE END OF THE ARDAS.
SAID IN EASY TIMES AND HARD.
TESTED BY NIGHTFALL IN THE CAMPS.
cards: Two words sit near the very end of the Ardas, just before the wish for the good of all: chardi kala. Sikhs say them to one another as well, in easy times and hard ones. On an easy day they can sound like a slogan.
But Sikhs remember decades when they were hunted and outnumbered, and in the stories of those camps, rising spirits had to mean something by nightfall. Today: chardi kala in the century.

teach.b: Sikhs translate chardi kala as rising spirits, or ever-ascending spirit. It isn't cheerfulness. It's a spirit that stays turned upward when everything outside is turned down.
Three things show what it meant in the hard century. First, the night prayer.

teach.h: KIRTAN SOHILA: THE CAMP IS THE HOUSE.
teach.b: Sikhs end the day with Kirtan Sohila, and its first hymn, by Guru Nanak, speaks of the house where the Creator's praises are sung and reflected on, and asks that the song of praise be sung there. That's in paraphrase.
The riders had no house. Tradition says they sang it anyway, quietly, in camps without lamps, and the camp became the house. Second, the Ardas.
The half-line before the good of all joins two things: Nanak's Name, and chardi kala.

teach.h: FROM THE NAME, NOT FROM MOOD.
teach.b: In the prayer, rising spirits come from the Name, not from mood. A rider didn't have to feel brave; he had to keep remembering. Third, the humor, the same camp speech the Nihangs still keep.

Tradition says the camps joked about their own hardship, giving poor things grand names, laughing at hunger rather than letting it win. Joking about yourself while the world tries to erase you is its own kind of courage.

teach.h: A JOKE AT YOUR OWN EXPENSE.
teach.b: A song at night, a Name to lean on, a joke at your own expense. None of it changed the danger. It changed how they carried it.
Hunted for decades, they still sang.

how: Sikhs recite Kirtan Sohila before sleep, and the Ardas closes with a wish for chardi kala through the Name and the good of all; Sikhs greet hardship with the phrase chardi kala as an ideal of spirit.

o: rising spirits that stay turned upward
the night prayer said before sleep
cheerful good luck that comes on easy days

p: a joke at your own expense

s: chardi kala just means being cheerful
it's a spirit that stays turned upward, and the Ardas ties it to the Name.
the riders sang the night prayer even in hiding
tradition says they sang Kirtan Sohila quietly, and the camp became the house.
you have to feel brave to have chardi kala
in the Ardas, rising spirits come from the Name, from remembering, not from mood.

games.q: your band has eaten nothing but dry bread for days. someone asks how everyone's doing. what's the chardi kala answer?
o: give the poor meal a grand name, laugh, and keep remembering the Name.
games.why: tradition says the camps joked about their hardship, giving poor things grand names, and the Ardas ties chardi kala to the Name, not to a full stomach.

practice: Choose a line you know that lifts you: a hymn, a verse, a song from childhood, or, if you pray, Waheguru said slowly. Hum or say it under your breath, once, then again, quietly, the way it would sound in a camp with no lamps.
If nothing in you rises, that's fine; they sang either way.

wordCard.voice: chardi kala, rising spirits that came from the Name, kept in the camps with a night prayer and a joke at their own expense. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi for chardi kala, rising or ever-ascending spirits.

carryVoice: Your line: they still sang. Even with no lamps, the camp became the house. Day eight hundred eighty-three, done.
